items.title: [popsci.com] Nearby giant likely tilted hot Jupiter out of view
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Astronomers say the hot Jupiter TOI-2535 b, about 1,000 light-years away, stopped transiting its star in March 2026 because the gravitational pull of a nearby, still-unseen planet tilted its orbit out of Earth’s line of sight. NASA’s Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite observed the system from April 2019 to March 2026; the planet circles its star every 8.25 days. Before the transits vanished, they arrived as much as six hours early or late and grew shorter and shallower, signs that the orbit’s alignment was changing. How the planet moved close to its star remains uncertain. The study appeared in *The Astrophysical Journal Letters* on Nov. 9. TOI-2535 b is not expected to transit again for at least 30 years, while its companion could become visible in transit sooner.

items.title: [sci.news] Chinese fossils extend Homo erectus survival and reveal rainforest adaptation
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Two studies published in Nature on Nov. 18 report that Homo erectus lived in southern China far later than previously documented and inhabited tropical rainforest there. Nine fossil teeth from Naxian and Baxian caves in Guangxi date to 324,000–184,000 years ago. Researchers identified eight as Homo erectus, extending its known mainland Asian record by roughly 200,000 years. A ninth tooth, PA1796, does not match Homo erectus, Neanderthals or modern humans. Researchers cannot yet tell whether it belonged to a Denisovan or another hominin. Its presence suggests at least two human groups inhabited the region during the period represented by the finds. Chemical evidence from the teeth and animal fossils indicates that the Homo erectus individuals lived in a rainforest ecosystem, challenging the idea that only Homo sapiens could use such habitats. Strontium signatures also suggest some individuals moved across a wide area as children. Researchers continue searching southern China’s caves for fossils that could help identify the mystery tooth and clarify the species’ history.

items.title: [science.nasa.gov] Webb traces Andromeda star merger, challenging common-envelope models
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Astronomers say a smaller star spiraled into a red giant and merged with it in the Andromeda galaxy, marking the first closely tracked observation of this stage of binary-star evolution. The system, named AT 2025abao, brightened over several years before erupting in October 2025. NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope observed it 47 days after the outburst peaked, helping researchers reconstruct the event. The team estimates that the giant had seven times the Sun’s mass and the companion about 0.7 times the Sun’s mass. Their interaction ended after about seven orbits, or seven years. The findings, published in Nature on Nov. 18, indicate that energy transport during the shared-envelope phase may be more complex than standard models describe. Researchers say continued observations are needed to determine the remnant’s state and confirm the merger.

items.title: [tuoitre.vn] European Hera probe begins examining asteroid struck in NASA deflection test
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

The European Space Agency’s Hera spacecraft has begun surveying the Didymos asteroid pair from about 25 to 30 kilometers away, four years after NASA deliberately struck the smaller asteroid, Dimorphos, to test asteroid deflection. Hera’s first images show Didymos from a new angle, revealing boulders, craters and ridge-like features; some rocks may have been blasted from Dimorphos and traveled about 1 kilometer to the larger asteroid. The 2022 impact shortened Dimorphos’ orbit around Didymos by about 32 to 33 minutes and also altered the pair’s path around the sun. Hera’s close-up investigation aims to determine how the impact changed Dimorphos and why the deflection was greater than simulations predicted. The probe is expected to begin closer, more detailed observations next month, using 25 instruments and two CubeSats that will survey Dimorphos and attempt to land there.

items.title: [popsci.com] Chad study finds eagles may prey on 26-kilogram baboons
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Researchers have found marks on bones and skulls suggesting Verreaux’s eagles preyed on adult male olive baboons in Chad’s Ennedi Plateau, including one estimated to have weighed 26.2 kilograms. The study, published Nov. 18 in the American Journal of Biological Anthropology, challenges a longstanding rule of thumb that primates above about 13 kilograms were effectively beyond avian predation. Previously, no primate heavier than that had been confirmed killed by a raptor. The team documented punctured eye sockets and talon-like scrapes on shoulder blades among the baboon remains. It did not witness a kill, so the researchers describe eagle predation as a likely explanation rather than a directly observed event. Some early hominins were in a similar weight range, but the findings do not establish that eagles hunted adult hominins or influenced their defensive behavior. The researchers plan further study of the isolated baboon population and its behavior.

items.title: [nasa.gov] Voyager 1 stops sending science data before one-light-day milestone
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

NASA’s Voyager 1 has stopped sending science and engineering data, though its carrier signal remains detectable, the agency said as it confirmed the spacecraft reached one light-day from Earth on Nov. 18. Launched in 1977, the probe is now more than 16 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers) away in interstellar space; its signal took 24 hours to reach Earth. The spacecraft has sent no data since Nov. 14. Engineers are investigating the fault. NASA said a similar interruption in 2023 was traced to an onboard computer, while the current issue may also involve the computer that collects and formats instrument readings. The carrier signal shows the spacecraft is still transmitting and allowed engineers to verify its distance, but it does not provide the missing science readings. Voyager project manager Suzanne Dodd said the team remains in contact with the probe. Because signals take a day each way, sending a command and receiving a response now takes about two days, slowing efforts to diagnose the fault and restore the data flow.

items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Researchers report that a Neanderthal-derived DNA variant is associated with a smaller occipital lobe and lower odds of schizophrenia in modern humans. In UK Biobank data, each copy of the variant corresponded to about 0.85 cubic centimeters less occipital-lobe volume; people with two copies had nearly 10% lower odds of schizophrenia than those with no copies. The occipital lobe processes visual information. The variant lies near DAAM1, a gene involved in brain development, but researchers have not established how it affects the brain or whether the smaller lobe explains the schizophrenia association. The variant was not associated with a meaningful difference in intelligence, and outside researchers cautioned against drawing conclusions about Neanderthal brain function from the findings in modern humans. The study was published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. Its authors say further work, including studies using brain organoids or animal models, could investigate the mechanism.

The North Atlantic right whale population fell to an estimated 382 animals at the end of 2025, down seven from the revised 2024 estimate, according to the North Atlantic Right Whale Consortium. The roughly 2% decline followed several years of slow growth. Scientists say the whales remain exposed to fishing-gear entanglements and vessel strikes as they migrate between Canadian and U.S. waters. The 2025-26 calving season produced 24 calves, the most since 2009. Researchers documented two whale deaths and eight human-caused injuries in 2026. Canada launched a whale-safe fishing gear strategy in February, while the U.S. House passed a bill to extend a pause on new protections for lobster and crab fisheries through 2035. The bill awaits Senate action.

About 20 Indigenous Awá living in isolation approached the Guajajara village of Tawari on Monday, November 16, in Arariboia Indigenous Territory, in the Brazilian state of Maranhão; they received yams and returned to the forest. Members of the Guajajara community recorded the encounter, and the organization Survival International shared the footage. The National Foundation for Indigenous Peoples (Funai) and Indigenous health personnel are in the area. The government activated an emergency coordination mechanism to assess the situation and health risks. Authorities said they are still assessing the initial information and that this isolated approach does not mean the Awá have abandoned their isolation. The reason for the visit has not been confirmed; Survival International linked it to pressure from illegal loggers, hunters, and ranchers on the territory. The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) says a strengthening El Niño could reach record strength by December and intensify heat and disruptive rainfall patterns into 2027. In its 2026 climate update, the agency reported that global temperatures from January through September averaged about 1.47°C above the preindustrial level and said 2026 is on track to rank among the four warmest years on record. Human-caused warming is adding to the risks associated with the naturally occurring climate pattern. The World Health Organization (WHO) has classified the expected health effects as an emergency for the first time for an El Niño event and published a plan for a Grade 3 preparedness response requiring major to maximal efforts. The agency warns that heat, drought and heavy rain can increase risks of heat illness, food insecurity and infectious disease, with vulnerable and conflict-affected communities facing particular danger. The WMO says the event is on track to reach record strength by December; its climate update uses data through September and does not include the latest impacts.

items.title: [cbc.ca] Alberta bill sets data-centre limits and well cleanup funds
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Alberta introduced Bill 42 on Nov. 18, proposing new siting and water rules for large data centres and mandatory cleanup funding for every new oil and gas well. Centres using at least 10 megawatts would generally have to be at least 600 metres from homes and avoid top-quality or irrigated farmland; they would also face a near-zero cooling-water standard. The Alberta Utilities Commission would regulate the larger facilities. The province says about 30% of current proposals could be affected, while projects already far along in approvals or construction would be exempt. For new wells, companies would pay up to $50,000 initially and make equal annual payments for up to 10 years. The money would remain attached to the well if ownership changes. If a well becomes orphaned, its funding would go to the Orphan Well Association. The requirements are expected to cover wells drilled after April 1, 2027. The bill would also eliminate Alberta’s oil-sands emissions cap, which the province says is redundant with industrial carbon pricing.

Centres using at least 10 megawatts would generally have to be at least 600 metres from homes and avoid top-quality or irrigated farmland; they would also face a near-zero cooling-water standard. The province says about 30% of current proposals could be affected, while projects already far along in approvals or construction would be exempt (cbc.ca, thestar.com). For new wells, companies would pay up to $50,000 initially and make equal annual payments for up to 10 years. The money would remain attached to the well if ownership changes. If a well becomes orphaned, its funding would go to the Orphan Well Association. The requirements are expected to cover wells drilled after April 1, 2027 (cbc.ca, thestar.com). The bill would also eliminate Alberta’s oil-sands emissions cap, which the province says is redundant with industrial carbon pricing (boereport.com). Meta project: The Sturgeon County complex is a $13-billion, one-gigawatt development expected to come online in two to three years (cbc.ca). Cleanup backlog: The Orphan Well Association lists 7,328 wells awaiting decommissioning and 9,258 sites needing reclamation; it estimates cleanup costs for its inventory at $1.66 billion (cbc.ca, thestar.com). Emissions cap: Bill 42 would eliminate the oil-sands emissions cap, which set a 100-million-tonne limit and had never been enforced; emissions were about 84 million tonnes in 2023 (boereport.com). Public response: A September CBC-commissioned poll found 31% of Albertans strongly opposed data-centre development and another 26% mostly opposed it, with electricity bills and environmental effects among the concerns (cbc.ca).

Perspective: Nathan Ip, Alberta NDP technology critic: Ip said the data-centre provisions do not set clear water-use standards and criticized the rules for exempting already approved projects; he called for a pause on projects while standards are developed (thestar.com, (The Toronto Star)
Perspective: Mark Daley, Western University chief AI officer: Daley said requiring operators to pay for their own power infrastructure is a substantial expense but can also improve electricity generation and transmission for the surrounding community (cbc.ca). (CBC News)
Perspective: Terry Schmidtke, Alberta Small Producers Group chair: Schmidtke said tying cleanup funding to wells through ownership transfers could make smaller producers more confident buying and selling wells while meeting closure obligations (cbc.ca). (CBC News)

items.title: [cbc.ca] B.C. flood alerts ease, but coastal surge and more rain pose risks
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

British Columbia downgraded or lifted many flood and rainfall alerts on Friday after days of heavy rain, but officials warned that more rain, unstable riverbanks and coastal flooding still posed risks through the weekend. The province’s River Forecast Centre kept high-streamflow advisories in place for the Sea-to-Sky, Howe Sound, North Shore and parts of Vancouver Island, while Environment Canada warned that high tides could exceed predicted levels in exposed coastal areas. Pemberton lifted an evacuation order for its Airport Road area and eased a shelter-in-place advisory, but the village remained under an evacuation alert. The Líl̓wat Nation lifted orders and alerts for most areas. Earlier flooding had blocked roads and prompted evacuation measures, including in Zeballos. Environment Canada reported 307 millimetres of rain in Port Mellon between Tuesday morning and Thursday at noon.

items.title: [arstechnica.com] FAA plans to replace floppy-based air traffic systems by 2028
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

The Federal Aviation Administration plans to replace four aging information systems that rely on floppy disks with a unified digital platform at 435 air traffic facilities by the end of 2028. The new Enterprise Information Display System, or E-IDS, will consolidate weather alerts, airport status and flight notices that controllers currently retrieve through outdated, often manual processes. The FAA says the platform will give controllers faster access to safety-critical information and reduce maintenance problems. The agency has already upgraded five sites, while Congress has provided $12.5 billion for broader air traffic control modernization. The FAA is seeking additional funding through the proposed Modern Skies Act. The agency plans to deploy the system at the remaining locations by the end of 2028.

The new Enterprise Information Display System, or E-IDS, will consolidate weather alerts, airport status and flight notices that controllers currently retrieve through outdated, often manual processes (arstechnica.com, techspot.com, theregister.com). The FAA says the platform will give controllers faster access to safety-critical information and reduce maintenance problems. The agency has already upgraded five sites, while Congress has provided $12.5 billion for broader air traffic control modernization. The FAA is seeking additional funding through the proposed Modern Skies Act (pcmag.com, theregister.com). The agency plans to deploy the system at the remaining locations by the end of 2028 (arstechnica.com). First locations: The five upgraded sites are Atlantic City, Nashville and Greater Rochester international airports, plus FAA data-processing hubs in Atlanta and Salt Lake City (techspot.com, pcmag.com). Systems replaced: E-IDS will replace IDS-4, ACE-IDS, NIDS and ERIDS, which separately provide weather, airport, airspace and en-route flight information (arstechnica.com, theregister.com). Safety record: A 2023 NOTAM system failure following the accidental deletion of a file temporarily halted domestic flight departures nationwide (theregister.com). Funding gap: The FAA says the proposed Modern Skies Act would provide $30 billion for modernization. A September Government Accountability Office report said the overhaul’s second phase needed a further $10.2 billion and had no completion date (theregister.com).
